summary: Drone delivery dispatchers work for operators such as Zipline, Wing, Amazon Prime Air or hospital and retail partners. They watch many autonomous aircraft beyond visual line of sight at once, assign orders to aircraft and nests, decide go/no-go on weather and airspace, and handle exceptions under FAA Part 135/107 approvals (with the proposed Part 108 BVLOS rule still pending) or EU U-space and SORA rules. AI helps most with shift briefings, triaging exceptions, writing incident and compliance reports, analysing delivery data, and explaining operations to the public, while the certificated people keep operational control.

prompts.title: Pre-shift go/no-go briefing
prompts.task: Turn raw weather, NOTAM and fleet data into a structured shift briefing
prompts.prompt: You are helping a drone delivery dispatcher prepare a pre-shift briefing for a BVLOS operation run under [FAA PART 135 / PART 107 WAIVER / EU SORA AUTHORISATION]. Here is the input: METAR/TAF [PASTE], NOTAMs and TFRs [PASTE], fleet status [PASTE: aircraft IDs, battery cycles, open maintenance items], and our operational limits from the ops manual [PASTE: wind, gust, visibility, precipitation, temperature limits]. Produce: 1) a table of each limit against the forecast for each hour of the shift, flagged GO / MARGINAL / NO-GO; 2) the airspace restrictions that affect our service area; 3) aircraft that should be held back, and why; 4) three items to watch. Quote the numbers you used. Do not make the final go/no-go call. List the assumptions the human must check.
prompts.caution: The pilot-in-command or certificated dispatcher makes the go/no-go decision; always check against official FAA/EASA sources and the approved ops manual.

prompts.title: Live exception triage
prompts.task: Rank simultaneous in-flight alerts during a busy delivery window
prompts.prompt: I am a drone delivery dispatcher monitoring [NUMBER] aircraft at once. These alerts have come in during the last [N] minutes: [PASTE ALERT LOG: aircraft ID, alert type, battery %, position/phase of flight, time]. Our standard contingency procedures are [PASTE OR SUMMARISE: return-to-nest, hold, divert to alternate landing site, flight termination criteria]. Rank the alerts by urgency in a table with these columns: aircraft, issue, likely cause, procedure that applies, time-critical deadline (such as battery reserve), and the recommended next human action. Mark any alert where the log is ambiguous and say what extra telemetry would resolve it. Keep the reply short enough to read in under one minute.
prompts.caution: Use this as decision support only. Follow the approved contingency procedures and do not delay a time-critical action while waiting for an AI reply.

prompts.title: Incident and occurrence report draft
prompts.task: Draft a factual incident report and check reporting obligations
prompts.prompt: Act as a safety reporting assistant for a drone delivery operator. Draft an internal occurrence report from these facts: [TIMELINE, AIRCRAFT ID, LOCATION, WEATHER, TELEMETRY SUMMARY, DAMAGE/INJURY, CREW ACTIONS]. Structure it as: summary, sequence of events, immediate actions, contributing factors (marked as confirmed or hypothesised), and follow-up items for our SMS. Separately, list which external reporting obligations might apply in [JURISDICTION]. Examples: in the US, 14 CFR 107.9 (10-day FAA report for serious injury or over $500 of damage) or NTSB 49 CFR Part 830; in the EU, Regulation (EU) 376/2014. For each one, give the trigger criteria and the deadline. Do not speculate about root cause beyond the evidence, and flag every point where legal review is needed.
prompts.caution: Reporting thresholds and deadlines must be checked against the current regulations and company counsel; the accountable manager signs off.

prompts.title: Delivery performance analysis
prompts.task: Find patterns in late, aborted and failed deliveries
prompts.prompt: You are an operations analyst for a drone delivery network. Here is [PERIOD] of delivery data as CSV: [PASTE: order ID, nest, destination zone, dispatch time, flight time, outcome (delivered/aborted/returned/failed), abort reason, wind, payload weight]. Analyse it and report: 1) on-time and completion rates by nest, zone and hour; 2) the top abort reasons and how they relate to weather and payload; 3) zones where we are close to our weather limits often enough to hurt reliability; 4) three operational changes to test, each with the metric that would show whether it worked. Show the calculations or code you used. State the sample sizes, and say where they are too small to conclude anything.
prompts.caution: Remove customer personal data, such as addresses and names, before pasting.

prompts.title: Community noise and privacy response
prompts.task: Reply to a resident complaint about drones over their neighbourhood
prompts.prompt: I am the dispatcher and community contact for a drone delivery service in [CITY/NEIGHBOURHOOD]. A resident wrote: [PASTE COMPLAINT]. Here are the facts about our operation: [ROUTES, ALTITUDES, FLIGHTS PER DAY, CAMERA USE AND DATA RETENTION POLICY, OPERATING HOURS, any route changes we could make]. Draft a reply of 150 to 200 words that is plain, accurate and not defensive. Explain what the resident is experiencing. Say which of their concerns we can address and how. Mention that aircraft broadcast Remote ID if that is true for us. Give a named contact channel. Do not promise changes that are not in the facts. Then list the internal follow-ups for my team, such as a route review or a noise measurement.
prompts.caution: Have communications or legal staff review commitments about privacy and data before you send the reply.

prompts.title: New service area readiness plan
prompts.task: Plan the operational and airspace steps to open a new delivery zone
prompts.prompt: Act as a planning assistant for a drone delivery operator expanding to [AREA], which lies [DISTANCE] from [AIRPORTS/HELIPADS/HOSPITALS]. We currently operate under [OUR APPROVALS: e.g. Part 135 certificate, Part 107 BVLOS waiver, or EASA specific category with SORA]. Produce a checklist-style readiness plan that covers: airspace class and the authorisations needed (e.g. LAANC or other FAA airspace authorisation, or U-space requirements in the EU); ground risk factors such as population density, roads and schools; nest and landing-site requirements; strategic deconfliction with other operators (ASTM F3548 UTM/USS where it applies); local stakeholder outreach; and dispatcher training. Flag which items depend on the proposed FAA Part 108 rule or other unsettled rules, and note any open questions.
prompts.caution: Regulatory requirements are changing quickly; confirm each item with the operator's compliance lead and the current FAA/EASA guidance.

prompts.title: Ops manual change impact check
prompts.task: Assess how a regulatory or procedure change affects dispatch practice
prompts.prompt: I am a drone delivery dispatcher. Our compliance team says [DESCRIBE CHANGE: e.g. new FAA rule text, updated waiver condition, revised Remote ID requirement, new internal limit]. Here are the relevant sections of our ops manual and dispatcher checklists: [PASTE]. Compare the two and produce a table with these columns: current procedure, what changes, affected checklist step or screen, training needed, and the effective date. Then write a 5-bullet briefing to read out at shift change. Quote the source text for each change. Where the change is ambiguous or the excerpt is incomplete, say so rather than guessing, and list the questions to send back to compliance.
prompts.caution: The compliance team's approved interpretation takes precedence; this is only a first-pass comparison.

prompts.title: Dispatcher upskilling plan
prompts.task: Build a study plan toward certification and BVLOS operations expertise
prompts.prompt: Act as a training mentor for someone moving from [CURRENT BACKGROUND, e.g. logistics dispatcher, Part 107 pilot, air traffic assistant] into drone delivery dispatch. Build a 12-week study plan with weekly goals covering: the Part 107 knowledge test (or EU A2/STS theory); airspace and weather interpretation; Part 135 operational control concepts; Remote ID and UTM basics (ASTM F3411, F3548); SORA and ground/air risk; human factors when monitoring many aircraft at once; and SMS and incident reporting. For each week, list free official resources (FAA, EASA, NASA UTM, ASTM summaries), one hands-on exercise, and 5 self-quiz questions. Note where the rules are still being written, such as the proposed Part 108.
prompts.caution: Check the resource links and current test requirements on official FAA/EASA sites.
